scenes.tts: The first film followed one gene. What changes when two genes travel through the same cross? The grid must track both allele pairs together.
scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's COLOR MAP: dominant alleles purple, recessive alleles white, grids green, probability markers yellow, neutral labels pale blue. Start with the earlier Pp grid, then slide in a second allele pair beside each parent. The grid stretches, still incomplete.
scenes.narration: The first film followed one gene. What changes when two genes travel through the same cross? The grid must track both allele pairs together.

scenes.visual: Hold the stretching grid. Title appears briefly: Two Genes, Sixteen Chances. Allele cards keep drifting at the edges.

scenes.tts: Mendel followed seed shape and seed color. We will use capital R and small r for shape. Capital Y and small y track color.
scenes.caption: Mendel followed seed shape and seed color. We will use R and r for shape. Y and y track color.
scenes.visual: Replace flower icons with large seed cartoons. Round and wrinkled shapes pulse beside R and r cards. Yellow and green fills pulse beside Y and y cards. Show symbols on screen, not molecular structures.
scenes.narration: Mendel followed seed shape and seed color. We will use R and r for shape. Y and y track color.

scenes.tts: Each parent is heterozygous for both genes. Every sex cell receives one shape allele and one color allele.
scenes.visual: Inside each large parent plant, show paired R/r cards above paired Y/y cards. During meiosis, one card from each row moves into each forming sex cell.
scenes.narration: Each parent is heterozygous for both genes. Every sex cell receives one shape allele and one color allele.

scenes.tts: In this model, the genes assort independently. Receiving either shape allele does not affect which color allele joins it. That creates every pairing.
scenes.visual: Build a two-branch choice tree. R and r form the first split; each branch splits again to Y and y. Mark the tree schematic, then connect its leaves to blank sex-cell circles.
scenes.narration: In this model, the genes assort independently. Receiving either shape allele does not affect which color allele joins it. That creates every pairing.

scenes.tts: Predict how many different sex-cell types this parent can make. Follow every path from a shape allele to a color allele.
scenes.visual: Keep the choice tree large. Hide the leaf labels behind pale-blue question cards. Yellow dots travel slowly down every branch and stop at the hidden leaves.
scenes.narration: Predict how many different sex-cell types this parent can make. Follow every path from a shape allele to a color allele.

scenes.visual: Hold the question. Yellow dots continue to glow at the four hidden leaves while the parent plants sway gently.

scenes.tts: The paths make capital R capital Y, capital R small y, small r capital Y, and small r small y. Each type is equally likely here.
scenes.caption: The paths make RY, Ry, rY and ry. Each type is equally likely here.
scenes.visual: Flip the leaf cards to reveal RY, Ry, rY and ry. Send a steady stream of each sex-cell type toward the top and left edges of the growing green grid.
scenes.narration: The paths make RY, Ry, rY and ry. Each type is equally likely here.

scenes.tts: Each sex cell carries one allele for each gene. No path carries both shape alleles or both color alleles from one parent.
scenes.visual: Inspect the four moving sex cells. Each opens to show exactly one shape card and one color card. Briefly reject two incorrect schematic cells carrying RR or Yy from one parent.
scenes.narration: Each sex cell carries one allele for each gene. No path carries both shape alleles or both color alleles from one parent.

scenes.tts: Place those sex-cell types along both sides. The square expands to show every possible meeting. Each box receives one type from each parent.
scenes.visual: Expand the carried grid into a large four-by-four layout. Row and column sex cells slide into place. Fill boxes with the combined genotypes, building diagonally so motion continues.
scenes.narration: Place those sex-cell types along both sides. The square expands to show every possible meeting. Each box receives one type from each parent.

scenes.tts: Read each box gene by gene. Combine the shape alleles first, then the color alleles. The finished genotype controls both visible traits.
scenes.visual: Zoom into one moving row-and-column meeting. Join R with r, then Y with y, forming RrYy. The seed icon beside it becomes round and yellow.
scenes.narration: Read each box gene by gene. Combine the shape alleles first, then the color alleles. The finished genotype controls both visible traits.

scenes.tts: Now group boxes by phenotype. A dominant shape allele makes round seeds. A dominant color allele makes yellow seeds in this model.
scenes.visual: Replace each genotype with a seed icon while retaining a faint genotype beneath. Round versus wrinkled shape transforms first; yellow versus green fill transforms second.
scenes.narration: Now group boxes by phenotype. A dominant shape allele makes round seeds. A dominant color allele makes yellow seeds in this model.

scenes.tts: The largest group is round and yellow. Two smaller groups carry one recessive phenotype. The smallest group is wrinkled and green.
scenes.visual: Boxes flow into four labeled bins. Show the computed on-screen ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 and fractions 9/16, 3/16, 3/16, 1/16. Keep numbers unspoken.
scenes.narration: The largest group is round and yellow. Two smaller groups carry one recessive phenotype. The smallest group is wrinkled and green.

scenes.tts: The smallest group needs recessive alleles at both genes. That combination occupies only the bottom corner of the organized grid.
scenes.visual: Dim all bins except wrinkled green. Trace its single rryy box back to the meeting of ry from both parents. Keep the full grid faintly visible for context.
scenes.narration: The smallest group needs recessive alleles at both genes. That combination occupies only the bottom corner of the organized grid.

scenes.tts: The ratio describes probabilities, not a promised batch. Random offspring can land unevenly. Larger samples usually settle closer to the predicted shares.
scenes.visual: Run a computed sampling animation from the four probabilities. A small seed counter jumps unevenly; a larger counter's four bars move closer to the expected dashed lines. Label curves computed.
scenes.narration: The ratio describes probabilities, not a promised batch. Random offspring can land unevenly. Larger samples usually settle closer to the predicted shares.

scenes.tts: Mendel's pea counts landed close, but not exactly on the predicted groups. That is what repeated chance events should look like.
scenes.visual: Transform the simulated bars into the lesson's observed dihybrid counts on screen: 315, 108, 101, 32. Overlay expected markers: 313, 104, 104, 35. Numbers remain visual only.
scenes.narration: Mendel's pea counts landed close, but not exactly on the predicted groups. That is what repeated chance events should look like.

scenes.tts: This pattern needs independent assortment and complete dominance. Linked genes, close together on one chromosome, can depart from it. Other allele relationships can change it too.
scenes.visual: Put a clear boundary around the carried grid labelled this model. Outside it, show a linked pair of cards traveling together and an intermediate-color seed, both labelled other cases.
scenes.narration: This pattern needs independent assortment and complete dominance. Linked genes, close together on one chromosome, can depart from it. Other allele relationships can change it too.

scenes.tts: One gene or two, the logic stays steady. Alleles separate, sex cells combine, and the square organizes the chances. Two independent genes simply give four sex-cell types and sixteen equal chances.
scenes.visual: Collapse the four-by-four grid beside the earlier two-by-two grid. Animate the same three-step arrow under both: separate, combine, organize. Seed counters continue changing beneath them.
scenes.narration: One gene or two, the logic stays steady. Alleles separate, sex cells combine, and the square organizes the chances. Two independent genes simply give four sex-cell types and sixteen equal chances.

scenes.visual: Show one centered line only: 'Genes that sort independently turn four sex-cell types into 9:3:3:1 chances.'
